comments.author: @JoeSmith-jd5zg
comments.text:
Tired of the "automation won't replace humans, but work with them" nonsense. Entry-level today, mid/late career tomorrow, C-suite the next day. Starting with the great decoupling in the 1970s, human labor has been and will continue trending to zero. Think EXPONENTIALLY, not LINEARLY. Automation and robotics will necessarily replace human workers due to the current economic system. Today, AI is the WORST it will ever be going forward. It DOESN'T MATTER if AI "creates" 200 million new jobs...AI will solve and execute these new "jobs" much faster than humans will be able to adapt, learn, and fill them. Capital/employee model-it worked great...for quite a while. However, now companies that automate lower their costs, become more competitive. Those that keep higher-cost human labor necessarily fall behind and will go out of business. This creates a system where replacing people with machines is not just likely, but necessary for company survival. There is a way to deal with this humanely, but it would require a full revamp of the social contract and our concept of work. Even capitalists will want this change when unemployment reaches a tipping point and there’s no one left with money to buy the crap they’re selling.

I know, LLMs are leveling off, "what about the energy?," blah, blah, blah. Do not conflate LLMs with AI. LLMs are no more AI than vacuum tubes are computers or AOL dial-up is the internet. So, LLMs are leveling off. History shows technological advance is not just one sigmoid curve. It's a series of sigmoid curves with each successive one reaching new capabilities and new heights. To think that after 200,000 years, this pattern is all the sudden going to stop is absurd. I also understand there will be new jobs for humans created, it will go in this pattern: Automation creates 5 new jobs this year, lays off 30; creates 5 new jobs next year, lays off 500; creates 5 new jobs the following year, lays off 1500 etc. In the macro economic picture, do you not see this as an issue? I also understand there is more opportunity for entrepreneurs. Again, from the macro perspective there is a MINORITY of people that have the entrepreneurial ability/spirit. It takes that, and a strong majority of people don't have it.

Reasoning AI Is the Next Big Leap. The future of AI is not just about generating answers, but about “reasoning” breaking down complex problems step-by-step, more like a human brain. Breakthroughs like DeepSeek’s open-source reasoning models are already being incorporated into platforms like GPT and xAI, marking a shift toward more advanced, thoughtful AI. Think EXPONENTIALLY, not LINEARLY.

There’s a persistent and misleading narrative circulating often perpetuated by short term goal-driven institutions like politicians, universities, and tech company executives, that the future of work is secure. The claim goes: “You just need to learn how to work with AI,” and humans collaborating with AI will outperform either one alone. But recent research, including a landmark study from the University of Virginia, tells a different story. In diagnosing medical conditions, AI alone achieved far greater accuracy than either human doctors or even doctors assisted by AI. The median diagnostic accuracy for the docs using Chat GPT Plus was 76.3%, while the results for the physicians using conventional approaches was 73.7%. Sounds like “a win” at first. However, Chat GPT Plus alone achieved a median diagnostic accuracy of more than 92%. In other words, the comforting idea that humans will always be essential partners to machines is crumbling. In many fields, AI is not just a tool, it is the superior performer. This has staggering implications for the future of work, especially to the often used solution of prior technological displacement that go “You just need to be retrained.” To the group advocating the "retraining solution," I pose to you this: You have a medical doctor, just finished 8 years of higher education, a low-paid 4-year internship/residency, is hundreds of thousands of dollars in debt, and just got outperformed by automation; what would you have this doctor retrained into that will offer a secure job?

The result of this, since the United States' moronic system is based on taxing employees for about 70% of all tax revenue, this will further exacerbate the problem. Tax needs to be based on what's going on now and in the future not what worked 75 years ago. Oh I know it's so evil to think, but we might need to tax the companies who are doing the automation. Even if you do that, it's a win-win. For instance say a company had 1,000 employees in automated away down to 100. 1,000 employees paid federal taxes, including payroll tax, of about 20 million a year. Now the 100 people pay about 2 million a year. However, by automating, the company sees two things: they are no longer paying approximately 60 million in wages and their share of payroll tax, AND since nobody automates to lose money they also have higher profits. What's so wrong about taxing that company for the $60 million dollars they don't have to pay anymore and a fair percentage of their additional profits they now make through the automation. Not all the additional profits, but some of them. If you do that there's a higher tax revenue and more profits for the company. That's a win-win for the government and for businesses. If humanity, as a whole, weren't so stupid, we would just adjust as tech progresses to where EVERYONE benefits somewhat from each stage and just move smoothly into the post-labor economy.

To understand this shift, consider the historical role of the horse and oxen. They were once essential to the economy as sources of power for agriculture, transport, and industry. Technologies like the horse collar and the steel plow dramatically increased their output, making them even more valuable. But then came the steam engine and, later, the internal combustion engine. These machines didn’t just help the horse, but outperformed it entirely. Trains, tractors, and trucks could do the job ten, even a hundred times faster and more powerfully. And from that moment forward, the horse was no longer critical to economic output. It was, in essence, unemployed.

This is what AI and robotics are doing to human labor. They are not simply replacing the repetitive or the physical; they are increasingly outperforming humans in cognition, strategy, design, and communication. And just like the horse, our value in the economic system will diminish, not from lack of talent or effort, but because machines will do the job better. That’s why we need to start thinking not in terms of retraining, but about restructuring society itself for a world where human labor is no longer essential to production. When the very essence of what makes an entity useful to the current economy is superseded (be that strength, endurance, dexterity, analysis, creativity, empathy, intelligence, persuasion as well as many other qualities) that entity becomes irrelevant to economic output.

Potential solution. Decentralized AI Ownership: A Bridge Toward Post-Scarcity. While Universal Basic Income (UBI) may serve as an initial economic stopgap, bridging today’s economy with tomorrow’s abundance consider an even more equitable and long-term solution: Decentralizing the ownership of artificial intelligence itself. 

Rather than concentrating the power of AI in the hands of a few corporations or governments, envision a model where AI entities are open-source and collectively owned. This could take the form of assigning each person a digital "share" of an AI system, not unlike a stakeholder’s share in a company. As the AI produces value, whether through intellectual labor, creative output, or autonomous economic participation, those shares would generate dividends distributed directly to individuals. 

This model would ensure that as AI becomes the dominant productive force in society, the wealth it creates is shared universally, not monopolized. It aligns with the principle that the fruits of public knowledge made possible by centuries of human collaboration should benefit everyone, not just a few early adopters or private entities. In practice, this could look like: 

- AI systems running Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAOs) that distribute profits algorithmically.
- Smart contracts ensuring transparent, equitable income flows based on collective stake.
- Global “AI cooperatives” where users vote on how AI is used, improved, and deployed.
- Universal basic compute.
 
If AI becomes the primary driver of economic output, then equitable access to its benefits isn’t just fair, it’s necessary to avoid deepening inequality and instability. It provides a scalable, technologically aligned extension to UBI, ensuring people not only have income, but true economic participation in the age of intelligent machines. 

Ultimately, decentralized AI ownership may be the last transition phase before full post-scarcity, when advanced technologies like universal nanofactories or matter compilers render even economic structures obsolete. Until then, however, models like this offer a way to reclaim agency in a world where production no longer requires human hands, and where wealth can, for the first time in history, truly be universal.

Im afraid that the AI usage will end up worsening skills in the long term as seeing the answer isnt the same as learning the answer. If you simply ask and use the answer you will never escape blooms taxonomy's level 1/2 (recall/understand) where the least amount of learning happens. In the past you had to evaluate (level 3) the sources you gathered, analyze their usage for your goal (level 4), and creatively (level 5) integrate it into your code. 

Each step up in that heirarchy of blooms taxonomy leads to exponentially more learning, more relationships between concepts created, per unit time. So, unless study technique becomes a core part of software dev the overall quality of devs will suffer massively.

In short, prompting =/= learning

comments.author: @fennecbesixdouze1794
comments.text:
AI has absolutely no hope of replacing developers, but it does stand a good chance of skyrocketing demand for developers.

If AI means more people build more software, that inevitably means there will be more software-exposed firms that need to hire developers to maintain and extend that software. The fact that LLMs produce *custom code* makes that even more true: since the code LLMs are producing is not standardized into a product (like no-code platforms or SaaS products), but is rather bespoke code, once it becomes so bloated and complex that the LLM can't handle it anymore, it will require human programmers to maintain and extend.

So: 
- the productivity of software developers will go way up, because they are able to produce more software with the assistance of AI
- the demand for software engineers will go way up, because more people will have custom bespoke code in need of human maintenance and extension
- the demand for software engineers will go way up, because firms newly entering software with LLM-generated code will discover new problems and contexts that are outside of the LLM's distribution

AI gets better by saturating their training distributions. They do not show any ability to get smarter beyond their training data, or generalize creative solutions to new problems outside their training data. But software engineering, at its vanguard, has always meant developing creative ways to solve new problems with software. If AI replaced all the software developers, it would mean all forward progress in software would halt: AI would be better than anyone at solving all our current problems, but completely unequipped to solve any future problems. For AI to continue being useful, it will always have to live alongside humans: learning from our creativity and saturating the new distributions that human creativity outputs.

comments.author: @jeffgros8508
comments.text: I would bet that most developers have been through at least one 'obselecense scare' already unless they are just out of school. I develop embedded systems. I used to write all the driver code myself (code that sets up clocks, controls SPI/UART, etc). Then the processor vendors started making code generators to configure the drivers. Just click some buttons and out comes the code! At first I rejected them because the code quality was bad. They improved a lot over a 5 year span. Now I use them for 80% of the driver code. They are still wasteful and slow, but they are sufficient if you just have to configure something once. And time to market is much faster. It sounds analogous to what happened long ago once developers switched from assembly to C. The compilers sucked at first, and now they are so good that in most cases its probably going to better than most people (including me). But you still might write an interrupt handler in assembly now and then.

comments.text:
This is exactly the point I’ve been thinking about.

AI may reduce the need for some kinds of entry-level coding work, but it does not eliminate the need for builders. It changes the path.

The new skill is not just “write code.” It is learning how to turn intent into working systems: asking better questions, reviewing what AI produces, understanding users, making technical tradeoffs, and shipping something real.

That is why I think the message to young engineers and new graduates should not be “you are doomed.” It should be: your path is changing, but you still have agency if you learn how to build with these tools instead of waiting for the old ladder to come back.

comments.text:
Scale is important here and often forgotten about in this conversation. When it comes to building a small, simple, synchronous application where you don't need to worry too much about security or privacy, then AI will do an amazing job.

But that's not what most large scale services are. Dealing with large volumes of concurrent requests, handling race conditions, security issues, service reliability, scaling within acceptable boundaries, being able to extend with additional features without breaking existing functionality, etc, etc. these aren't the extra stuff. This IS the product.

The fallacy in these conversations is that software engineers are "coders". Coding is the easiest part of the job. It was never the bottleneck. Software engineering is a problem solving profession.

AI won't replace engineers, it will empower engineers.

But the people making decisions don't understand this, they are making hiring/firing decisions based on technology they don't understand. Breaking the pipeline of grads/junior engineers coming into the industry is going to create a major problem a few years from now.

comments.author: @whattowatchrightnow
comments.text:
Everyone's panicking about AI killing software engineering. Oracle just cut 30,000 people. Must be the end, right?

Wrong. AI means more software, not less.

It's the Jevons Paradox. When you make something dramatically cheaper to produce, you don't get less of it. You get wildly more of it. Spreadsheets didn't kill accountants. They created a world where everyone does financial modeling.

Those 30,000 engineers aren't leaving software. They're being redistributed into the software economy with fewer institutional constraints and better tools than they've ever had.

Some will join startups where 3 people build what used to take 30. Some will go independent. Some will finally ship that sidequest they've been thinking about for years. Some will walk into healthcare or local government or construction and rebuild everything they touch.

Software engineers aren't fry cooks. They're ambitious, skilled people. Give them 100x leverage and they won't do 1/100th the work. They'll build things that weren't possible before.

The bottleneck was never ambition. It was bandwidth. AI just removed it.

The next five years won't be defined by engineers being replaced. It'll be defined by sidequests finally shipping.

Ask them the tradeoffs in their discissions. Better yet, ask them to explain anything about their app in depth. A lot of non Software Engineers think that coding is the job, but in reality coding is a small part of the job. We are not 'programmers', our titles are developer and engineer. There is a reason for that. There is a lot beyond coding that goes into being a Software Engineer; software architecture, requirements gathering, understanding the business domain, understanding the applications, and most importantly, developing maintainable and scalable systems with all of these things in mind. 

Look I am glad coding is more accessible to people who otherwise would have no exposure, but you cannot take anyone who 'vibe coded' an app and put them in a real Software Engineering role; they will absolutely drown. It’s like following a legal template you generated from an LLM. You might produce a document, but that doesn’t make you a lawyer who understands nuance, risk, and how to handle edge cases. LLMs can guide execution, but they don’t replace real world human judgment, experience, and context. 

This whole idea of 'AI taking jobs' narrative is purely marketing. LLMs aren’t magic. They’re probabilistic systems that generate text based on patterns in data and context. They don’t have true understanding, judgment, or real world accountability. You know, the things you need to actually do a job. They have reasoning like behavior, but it is not human reasoning.

comments.author: @JoeSmith-jd5zg
comments.text:
Tired of the "automation won't replace humans, but work with them" nonsense. Entry-level today, mid/late career tomorrow, C-suite the next day. Starting with the great decoupling in the 1970s, human labor has been and will continue trending toward zero. Think EXPONENTIALLY, not LINEARLY. Automation and robotics will necessarily replace human workers due to the current economic system. Today, AI is the WORST it will ever be going forward. It DOESN'T MATTER if AI "creates" 200 million new jobs...AI will solve and execute these new "jobs" much faster than humans will be able to adapt, learn, and fill them. Capital/employee model-it worked great...for quite a while. However, now companies that automate lower their costs, become more competitive. Those that keep higher-cost human labor necessarily fall behind and will go out of business. This creates a system where replacing people with machines is not just likely, but necessary for company survival. There is a way to deal with this humanely, but it would require a full revamp of the social contract and our concept of work. Even capitalists will want this change when unemployment reaches a tipping point and there’s no one left with money to buy the crap they’re selling.

I know, LLMs are leveling off, "what about the energy?," blah, blah, blah. Do not conflate LLMs with AI. LLMs are no more AI than vacuum tubes are computers or AOL dial-up is the internet. So, LLMs are leveling off. History shows technological advance is not just one sigmoid curve. It's a series of sigmoid curves with each successive one reaching new capabilities and new heights. To think that after 200,000 years, this pattern is all the sudden going to stop is absurd. I also understand there will be new jobs for humans created, it will go in this pattern: Automation creates 5 new jobs this year, lays off 50; creates 5 new jobs next year, lays off 900; creates 5 new jobs the following year, lays off 15,000 etc. In the macro economic picture, do you not see this as an issue? I also understand there is more opportunity for entrepreneurs. Again, from the macro perspective there is a MINORITY of people that have the entrepreneurial ability/spirit. It takes that, and a strong majority of people don't have it.

Reasoning AI Is the Next Big Leap. The future of AI is not just about generating answers, but about “reasoning” breaking down complex problems step-by-step, more like a human brain. Breakthroughs like DeepSeek’s open-source reasoning models are already being incorporated into platforms like GPT and xAI, marking a shift toward more advanced, thoughtful AI. Think EXPONENTIALLY, not LINEARLY.

There’s a persistent and misleading narrative circulating often perpetuated by short term goal-driven institutions like politicians, universities, and tech company executives, that the future of work is secure. The claim goes: “You just need to learn how to work with AI,” and humans collaborating with AI will outperform either one alone. But recent research, including a landmark study from the University of Virginia, tells a different story. In diagnosing medical conditions, AI alone achieved far greater accuracy than either human doctors or even doctors assisted by AI. The median diagnostic accuracy for the docs using Chat GPT Plus was 76.3%, while the results for the physicians using conventional approaches was 73.7%. Sounds like “a win” at first. However, Chat GPT Plus alone achieved a median diagnostic accuracy of more than 92%. In other words, the comforting idea that humans will always be essential partners to machines is crumbling. In many fields, AI is not just a tool, it is the superior performer. This has staggering implications for the future of work, especially to the often used solution of prior technological displacement that go “You just need to be retrained.” To the group advocating the "retraining solution," I pose to you this: You have a medical doctor, just finished 8 years of higher education, a low-paid 4-year internship/residency, is hundreds of thousands of dollars in debt, and just got outperformed by automation; what would you have this doctor retrained into that will offer a secure job?

The result of this, since the United States' moronic system is based on taxing employees for about 70% of all tax revenue, this will further exacerbate the problem. Tax needs to be based on what's going on now and in the future not what worked 75 years ago. Oh I know it's so evil to think, but we might need to tax the companies who are doing the automation. Even if you do that, it's a win-win. For instance say a company had 1,000 employees in automated away down to 100. 1,000 employees paid federal taxes, including payroll tax, of about 20 million a year. Now the 100 people pay about 2 million a year. However, by automating, the company sees two things: they are no longer paying approximately 60 million in wages and their share of payroll tax, AND since nobody automates to lose money they also have higher profits. What's so wrong about taxing that company for the $60 million dollars they don't have to pay anymore and a fair percentage of their additional profits they now make through the automation. Not all the additional profits, but some of them. If you do that there's a higher tax revenue and more profits for the company. That's a win-win for the government and for businesses. If humanity, as a whole, weren't so stupid, we would just adjust as tech progresses to where EVERYONE benefits somewhat from each stage and just move smoothly into the post-labor economy.

To understand this shift, consider the historical role of the horse and oxen. They were once essential to the economy as sources of power for agriculture, transport, and industry. Technologies like the horse collar and the steel plow dramatically increased their output, making them even more valuable. But then came the steam engine and, later, the internal combustion engine. These machines didn’t just help the horse, but outperformed it entirely. Trains, tractors, and trucks could do the job ten, even a hundred times faster and more powerfully. And from that moment forward, the horse was no longer critical to economic output. It was, in essence, unemployed.

This is what AI and robotics are doing to human labor. They are not simply replacing the repetitive or the physical; they are increasingly outperforming humans in cognition, strategy, design, and communication. And just like the horse, our value in the economic system will diminish, not from lack of talent or effort, but because machines will do the job better. That’s why we need to start thinking not in terms of retraining, but about restructuring society itself for a world where human labor is no longer essential to production. When the very essence of what makes an entity useful to the current economy is superseded (be that strength, endurance, dexterity, analysis, creativity, empathy, intelligence, persuasion as well as many other qualities) that entity becomes irrelevant to economic output.

Potential solution. Decentralized AI Ownership: A Bridge Toward Post-Scarcity. While Universal Basic Income (UBI) may serve as an initial economic stopgap, bridging today’s economy with tomorrow’s abundance consider an even more equitable and long-term solution: Decentralizing the ownership of artificial intelligence itself. 

Rather than concentrating the power of AI in the hands of a few corporations or governments, envision a model where AI entities are open-source and collectively owned. This could take the form of assigning each person a digital "share" of an AI system, not unlike a stakeholder’s share in a company. As the AI produces value, whether through intellectual labor, creative output, or autonomous economic participation, those shares would generate dividends distributed directly to individuals. 

This model would ensure that as AI becomes the dominant productive force in society, the wealth it creates is shared universally, not monopolized. It aligns with the principle that the fruits of public knowledge made possible by centuries of human collaboration should benefit everyone, not just a few early adopters or private entities. In practice, this could look like: 

- AI systems running Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAOs) that distribute profits algorithmically.
- Smart contracts ensuring transparent, equitable income flows based on collective stake.
- Global “AI cooperatives” where users vote on how AI is used, improved, and deployed.
- Universal basic compute.
 
If AI becomes the primary driver of economic output, then equitable access to its benefits isn’t just fair, it’s necessary to avoid deepening inequality and instability. It provides a scalable, technologically aligned extension to UBI, ensuring people not only have income, but true economic participation in the age of intelligent machines. 

Ultimately, decentralized AI ownership may be the last transition phase before full post-scarcity, when advanced technologies like universal nanofactories or matter compilers render even economic structures obsolete. Until then, however, models like this offer a way to reclaim agency in a world where production no longer requires human hands, and where wealth can, for the first time in history, truly be universal.

comments.author: @roysegall2570
comments.text:
The "Wolt-ification" of AI is coming. When Wolt first launched, it was cheap AF. Everyone hyped it up because it felt like a steal, but they were just burning cash to get a "foot in the door." Once they became dominant, the prices spiked and people started abandoning the app.

We’re seeing the exact same play with AI orchestration, but with a much scarier "Physical Triangle" of costs:

The Electricity Bill: Running these models is a massive, growing drain on the power grid.

Hardware Demand: The price for GPUs, RAM, and chips is surging because physical supply can’t keep up.

The Complexity Gap: AI orchestration isn't just software; it's a massive, physical infrastructure expense.

This is an unequal triangle. The cost to run the "brain" is rising faster than the value it provides for basic tasks. Something has to give in 2026—either subscriptions triple in price, or companies stop using AI as the "main tool" for everything.

Remember: the bill always comes due—there’s no magic in the real world.

comments.author: @JamesMcGhee
comments.text:
If you call yourself an “engineer” and don’t verify the work you put your name on, you are not an engineer, you are a programmer or a “prompt jockey.” An engineer, in any discipline, exists to take responsibility for outcomes, ensure proper processes are followed, and provide stakeholders with the confidence to make strategic decisions based on that work.

In my professional opinion, tools like these, like all tools before them, simply reinforce software engineering’s position as a core engineering discipline. The low-effort tasks these tools trivialise do not diminish the value I bring to projects. I have proven that over decades, even as new tools emerged claiming to make software engineers irrelevant. Typing commands is not the core of my function; it is something I can do and enjoy, but it is not why I am paid.

Many times in my career I have warned companies against cutting corners. I have also welcomed them back when they ignored that advice, made critical mistakes, and required an engineer to fix them. I have worked in this industry from the ground up, and for multiple companies I have taught why investing in entry-level engineers, upskilling them, and cultivating an engineering division is essential. Your engineering team is your core asset in a technology-driven world. You can outsource it or build it internally, but there is no shortcut.

I still think the biggest issue is this framing of "getting rid of / reducing the boiler plate".

No, that is not what is happening.  The boilerplate has not been the only thing delegated to LLMs. Its the general structure / architecture of a project that the boilerplate represented that is getting delegated. 

The fundementall understanding of how the project is structured / set up. 

Yes, the "boring bits" of a project are, in fact, boring. 

But if you do not understand how the framework of a building is set up, you cant make a cool skyscraper with the security / knowledge that it wont collapse due to faulty foundations. 

It seems to be the one thing folk are not shouting about as, to be blunt, we are humans and we are lazy. We allow LLMs to do the "boring bits" and, even for the biggest critics, are ignoring the fact its that part of the project that is most susceptible to massive issues it done incorrectly.

comments.text:
As a senior developer, who has written 100000s line of code, who really understands code, you are able to understand and review the code generated by AI. Ok. But as a junior dev, if you start with AI - or you are even forced by your company to use AI to generate the code, you don't even have the chance to learn what code is good and what to avoid (although it works fine with normal usecases and passes all tests). But since now AI replaces especially juniors - who can become seniors in future?
What's even more important: Manager - of which most have no clue of coding - want to make software development much cheaper and faster. AI can do that. As a manager you finally can fire most of your devs and make more profit while even more software can get produced and shipped. That's the only thing which matters.
I would no longer learn to code, I consider it useless now, especially if you consider that AI is getting better each week. In a few years it might even outperform senior devs.
But what about quality? I need to admit, that I even don't know if AI generated code is better or worse of code developed by humans. In the area, where I work (SAP, ABAP), AI can't be used (yet), hence I never have used it. But what I know is, that most companies do not really care about quality. If I look at Windows it seems to get worse and worse and no one cares. Even the consumer don't seem to care, they only want many features as fast as possible.

comments.text:
A very interesting perspective.
However, I have to add a perspective of my own:

I worked in the tech industry as a software engineer for 25 years, when it really was complex and a lot of tech was very new and emerging (1980s - 2000s).
I no longer work as a software engineer (I'm old now and have had to accept new cohorts of fresh techies year-on-year, who need their own space and deserve the same opportunities I have enjoyed).
Nonetheless, I recall very clearly how much we engineers would work *together* on projects, face-to-face and in harmony when working to deadlines vs. market/customer demands.

Notwithstanding the obvious social and emotional support inherent in that practice, the collective (human) intelligence, brainstorming and the joy of reaching a useful, productive consensus cannot be replaced by A.I. within the coding cycle. Our products were always better when a team had some democratic involvement in the whole process; and, equally important, others in departments such as design and illustration, data analysis and production, would provide insights to such an extent that one could sometimes almost feel the contributions of all involved shining through the product itself at runtime.

I am neither convinced that A.I. can replace the human condition (as flawed as that is) and its important contribution to products that are mostly intended for people to use; or that A.I. cannot take a really impressive run at it.

A much more damning concern is those who really hold the cards. The Revenge of the Nerds period of the 70s, 80s and to a lesser extent the 90s, is largely over. But this is not for want of trying to immerse oneself in the joy of creativity, but simply because those who *do* hold the best (financial) hand today are those who are proudly such rabid money machinists.

Thank you for your time and insights. Your video is interesting and opens the debate on this topic.

What is needed now, though, is the debate ... globally and with strong cooperation.

Creativity and technology are very strong bedfellows. This is such an important part of what it means to be human that it is worth taking a strong resistive stance.

A.I. really could, and very much should, make all our lives better and more frictionless. What it must not be allowed to do is displace people ... people who need purpose, belonging and a common goal.

As long as Mr. and Mrs. $$$ call the shots - no matter that they will lead entire nations into universal darkness - we will never find genuine, lasting purpose and meaning again going forward.

If A.I. does manage to displace enough people, then there will be a terrible divide between wealthy maggots hiding behind <euphemism-alert> Mummy's apron <\euphemism-alert> and those who value their time and enjoy spending it making a genuinely creative contribution to the world.

Given A.I. feeds on input, and every request for assistance to an A.I. system is throwing more meat to this hungry, unemotional hound:

    I wonder, if perhaps as only a thought experiment, what A.I. would feed on if we all stopped bloody feeding it ... like Lemmings naively marching towards a cliff edge ... ?!

TTFN

comments.author: @gledatelj1979
comments.text:
The video correctly identifies that the current AI workflow is collaborative, requiring significant human input and review, and that "vibe coding" currently hits its limits on complex apps [03:14]. However, this is not a fundamental limitation of AI; it is an artifact of today's finite parameters and limited tokens.The video's claim that AI-generated code must be reviewed and refactored by a human to ensure it is "correct [and] maintainable" [05:05] is a classic misunderstanding of scaling laws in LLMs.The AI lacks the architectural wisdom to manage complexity, forcing the engineer to view the code itself as the value [05:52] and perform the high-level system design.

This perceived lack of architectural wisdom is simply a function of an insufficient parameter count.  Today's models operate in the 100-billion to trillion-parameter range. As future models scale to trillions of parameters, their ability to abstract, predict, and maintain large-scale system consistency will fundamentally exceed any single human architect. The 'complexity limit' the speaker hits is not a ceiling, but a checkpoint.  The fact is that the human's most efficient role is not to review lines of code, but to define the high-level system outcome and manage the AI's deployment pipeline.  The massive parameter count grants the AI Super-Refactoring capability, making human reorganization efforts obsolete and comparatively inefficient.

The video argues that raw code is the most efficient and "precise" way to understand system behavior [05:59], superior to any AI summary or explanation.
The AI can lose context or "misunderstand" a requirement in a complex prompt [06:26], forcing the engineer to read the code as the ultimate source of truth. This is why human coding skill is deemed indispensable [12:09]. The need for the human to read the code is a direct result of a constrained token context window. Today's models can only hold a fraction of a large codebase in their "working memory" at any given time. As context windows grow to millions of tokens, the AI will be able to ingest the entire codebase, all documentation, and the full history of interactions—creating a knowledge state that is inherently more precise and complete than the isolated human developer's understanding.In the future of true vibecoding, the human is the least efficient component for precision. The AI's internal token representation of the entire system will be the absolute source of truth. Trying to read thousands of lines of code to check the AI's work is a low-resolution bottleneck when the AI is capable of operating at the highest resolution of system knowledge.


Your conclusion that engineers must "learn AI and learn how to code" [12:34] is backward. It anchors the future of development in yesterday's inefficiencies.
From a futurist perspective, the current limitations are engineering problems, not philosophical ones. Once parameters grant the AI necessary architectural intelligence, and tokens grant it perfect system context, the "most efficient" way forward will not be human collaboration (as described at [02:31]), but pure, unadulterated, black-box Vibecoding. The job of the future is not coding with AI, but prompting and managing the AI system, where the human's focus shifts from the code to the business goal.

This is point on. The jobs change, but they don't disappear.

It's like the fear of bookkeepers, that the computer will lead to massive reduction in bookkeepers, because the majority of their work is calculating and writing things down.
Suddenly, bookkeepers were much more efficient doing this.
But instead of less bookkeepers, we got more. Because they now were able to expand bookkeeping from "purely passive keeping" to "actively optimizing". Suddenly, the bookkeeping expanded into controlling. And companies were able to reduce stock due to active stock management. And so on. 


This is the same in basically every application of a new technology. It changes, it doesn't replace. And for 5 industrial revolutions, it always caused more employment and more productive employment.

PS: Of course there are certain applications, where AI can in fact reduce a lot of the workforce. But all these jobs are jobs where you have a finite workload. 
For example doctors checking MRT pictures. There are only a certain number of MRTs needed. And now, with AI being really perfect to check these, you only need 1 remote doctor, to check the AI results instead of doing the checking themselves. This reduces the workload by 95%. This actually reduces the need for MRT doctors. But do you really think, these doctors will become unemployed? Or will they rather just become other types of doctors?

comments.text:
You're really an optimist. That's nice. Unfortunately, probably not a realist. (An optimist is someone who doesn't see things as tragically as they really are 😆)

AI will in the future take over the work of many people and cause unemployment to grow enormously. The fact that this isn't the case yet is no argument whatsoever that it can't be the case in the coming years.

You say that AI's tendency to give wrong answers rather than no answer at all. Yes it is a real effect — at the moment. But this has already improved dramatically, see Anthropic. The reason for this is largely already understood and lies in flawed reward strategies during the training phases. That will soon be a thing of the past.

You say that AI makes too many mistakes to be trusted. That's why it couldn't replace people. Seriously? Then why are there so many employees who make mistakes and still don't get fired? Because making mistakes is human? 😆😆😆

Because humans make mistakes, we have tests, development processes, bureaucratic approval processes, elaborate reviews, test engineering, unit tests, integration tests, system tests, tracing, logging, quality monitoring, and so on. The fact that the coding process is error-prone has never stopped investors throughout the history of software development from hiring coders. Why should that be the case with AI coders? 

Sure, you need human oversight and control, but AI makes coding so much easier that you need fewer people to do the same work. And a brief look back at history helps too: of course automated looms require human operators and technicians, but right after the invention of the power loom, 70% of weavers lost their jobs. There aren't many weavers today either — do you even know one? The profession has been virtually wiped out. Something similar applies to agriculture. Two hundred years ago, 90% of the population worked in farming. Then came agricultural machinery.

comments.author: @puregameplay4243
comments.text:
Interesting. I was playing around with Codex and built a Rubik’s Cube simulator with it. Funny thing: in the first few runs, it messed up face culling and needed a hint to fix it. It looked like the AI didn’t really understand 3D space in that case.

Still, the entire process was about 2–3 times faster than if I had built the whole thing myself. Software engineering is definitely going to change.

I think current LLMs are extremely useful knowledge-retrieval tools, with the added advantage that they can directly apply that knowledge. They still lack depth and attention to detail, though, because they compress knowledge into an abstract language layer. It’s similar to learning from another human: the original source has the full details, but communicates them through an abstraction protocol called human language. The recipient then has to “decompress” that information and reconstruct the underlying understanding.

comments.author: @JibunnoKage-YouTube-Channel
comments.text: Come on!  Of course the limit is 100M or about 325 FT.  And.. the CAT8 did not work.. because the signal resistance is higher than the CAT6... basic physics.  We run into this all the time with POE driven studio cameras... that push 10G over CAT6/A fine until we go very long distance...  We have a commercial grade production studio next to a house of worship, and have some very long cable runs to POE studio cameras.  The sub-ground cabling is about 150 to 160 FT CAT7A solid core, but the above ground at camera, and at studio receiver is stranded CAT 6A.  If we go over about 225 ft when positioning cameras, we lose quality, then speed, then signal.  The camera POE/Ethernet do NOT support switches in-between camera and receiver, use a custom Ethernet protocol stack, that is not complete ISO/OSI.  It drives 10G like crazy, but must be 1-to-1 connection.  Bummer is I don't yet find a 10G repeater!

comments.author: @neolithicnewbie
comments.text: Yep.  Once you exceed the 300ft (100m) limit the ethernet protocol falls apart. That length is due to the design that the smallest physical layer packet has to travel the entire length of the cable.  The only way to make ethernet longer is to do what Wang did with wangnet.  Make the minimum packet size larger so when it is sent out, it has time to reach every point in the cable length so it can be detected and any other device will wait to send it's message.  When you are using standard ethernet and have a longer cable than 100m, one transmitter could be sending a message and finish the message thinking it went out clean while another transmitter hadn't seen that message yet and started transmitting and trashing both messages.  Haven't read the original spec in a long time.  Maybe with your 350ft cable it's getting reflection and corrupting the transmitted message.

'Cuz I don't." - Dave, Notepad++ is a 3rd party "raw-dog" text editor, to use your words, with added features that benefit programmers and script writers, including auto-indent and code highlighting that recognizes a number of programming languages. (The latest version supports opening multiple files in tabs; I hope that doesn't kill it for the purists out there!) It doesn't replace an IDE's utility for large projects, but it's great for quick and dirty coding tasks. I've used it for writing Java code and batch command scripts. It's fast and fairly simple to use. Personally, I enjoy what the new Notepad has to offer and use Notepad++ for situations where I just want quick & dirty text files or need to write batch scripts. Although if you don't save your new Notepad-created files in the new .md format, quick & dirty text files are what you still get from it.

comments.author: @davidhawley1132
comments.text:
I've used GitHub Copilot to code signal processing in assembly on low-end MCUs.  You have to be able to understand and critique what it has written, but you don't need to know in advance the details of the MCUs you are using.  Without AI assistance, I probably would attempt less of this kind of project, and be less open to use unfamiliar MCUs.

Copilot seems to be optimized for output and minimizing thinking rather than quality.  The fact that it can produce reasonable quality can fool you into believing it will routinely perform at that level.  It also does better on very well known tools and tasks.

But in general, you've got to make sure (1) it has the vetted information that it needs and can access it, (2) justifies its output against that verified information, (3) and that it hasn't taken shortcuts (ask it).

comments.author: @mojloginjuzzajety4071
comments.text: @15:32 Gentlemen, this is the moment where digital meets analog :) The repeater will not really "boost" the Ethernet signal, it will regenerate it. The hard limit on the Ethernet copper is around 100m due to cable attenuation, close interference, far interference and, above 100 Mbit/s, where it is not serial, coherence. I would recommend using the old concentric cable (10 Mbit/s, no duplex) as it may go to 300m (officially 180m). Or... as You have PDP at home, maybe some good old "coaxial" - if I recall properly almost 500m? But, if we are to work in the XXI century: maybe an optic fibre for data and Ethernet cable just for power or a solar panel with battery?? That would also solve some risks as the longer the cable, the more fun a thunderstorm can introduce (even with shielding, as it is not so perfect against lightnings).

Beyond 100 meters, the signal is too weak for the receiving device to reliably interpret the data, leading to errors and packet loss.

Here's how I learn engineering, with intense assistance of AI: 

1. I let AI write a little feature.
2. I step through the code with the debugger, line by line, always asking: 
- what is happening here?
- what is its purpose? / Why can't it be omitted?
- what exactly is it that i don't understand?
3. As a rule, I have a list of questions now. I ask AI for the answers and insist about links in the official documentation.
4. I rebuild the feature again without AI, but with explaining comments.

This is how I learned to understand the Chi Framework for the Go Language very deeply.

It's slow, it's tedious, but it's worth it.

comments.text:
AI has not replaced developers; it has raised the bar for understanding, design, and long‑term thinking while making shallow, copy‑paste learning paths much less viable.
​

What actually caused the pain
The 2023–24 “AI panic” got blamed for layoffs, but most cuts came from over‑hiring, rising rates, and companies correcting after the 2020–22 boom, not from AI eliminating all dev work.
​

AI hype made many beginners think “learning to code” meant just prompting tools instead of building solid skills, which backfired once hiring got tighter.
​

How AI really changed dev work
AI now writes a big chunk of routine code, so value shifted from typing solutions to understanding architectures, trade‑offs, and how to make systems scale and survive in production.
​

Senior‑style thinking (debugging, design, edge cases, maintainability) became important much earlier in a dev’s journey, even for juniors.
​

The new risks for learners
The main danger is shallow understanding: shipping code you don’t really understand, over‑relying on AI, and never building the mental models needed to solve harder problems later.
​

The “easy path” of tutorials plus copy‑pasted AI answers might get you simple projects done but leaves you stuck when something breaks off the happy path.
​

Are junior jobs gone?
Junior roles are fewer and expectations are higher, but companies still need developers who can think, debug, and collaborate, not just prompt models.
​

Those who combine basics (HTML/CSS/JS, core backend concepts, debugging) with smart AI usage and real projects still have a path in.
​

What “learning properly” means now
You need consistent, hands‑on practice: building projects from scratch, breaking things, fixing them, and only then using AI as a helper instead of a crutch.
​

The winners in this new era are thoughtful engineers who understand why code works, can reason about systems, and use AI to go deeper—not to avoid thinking.
​

Thinking today that LLMs will replace programmers is like thinking 550 years ago that the printing press will replace authors. AI, when used right, is just mental scaffolding, much like numeracy and literacy was during the Axial Age or Arabic numerals and the printing press during early Modernity.

I think the crux is this: LLMs can generate code, but it is unclear as of now how that will play out in the long run. It may well be that much of the generated code is buggy in ways that are hard and therefore expensive to fix. And if LLM-generated code has to be tested to avoid such bugs, then those tests have to be written by somebody, which could easily turn into another bottleneck. I don't see a future where we have LLMs generate both code and tests and feel therefore convinced of the correctness of either one.

In short: Human-in-the-loop still seems indispensable. Maybe this will change but I think it's safe to predict it won't.

BTW, there's already research being done to connect LLMs to formal reasoning systems. Paradoxically, this could lead to a resurgence of classic symbolic AI. Time to start learning Prolog, maybe?

comments.text:
The video assumes the valuable thing a human brings is coding skill, and AI multiplies that. That's the wrong model.  

Domain expertise — the deep understanding of why a system works, not just how to type it — is what AI can't replace. When I bring 43 years of real-world experience to the table, AI becomes an engineering team executing my vision rather than a tool making a coder faster. That's not 10x productivity. That's one person doing work that a room full of engineers still couldn't do without that domain knowledge directing them.

What also gets overlooked is intentional design for self-correction. Most systems fail silently or with vague errors. Building a system that explicitly signals the boundary of its own knowledge — and hands you a precise starting point for diagnosis — means you're not debugging after the fact. The system identifies its own gaps in real time and tells you exactly where to look. You eliminate one factor at a time until only one explanation remains.

That combination — irreplaceable domain expertise driving AI implementation, with self-correcting diagnostic capability built in from the start — is what this video never considered. This video talks about developers and coders. This is architecture.

So no you do not need to be a coder, or a developer, because neither has what I have as an IT Professional to use AI to replace entire teams of Software Engineers.   There's Junior developers, there's Senior developers, but what there is not is my domain expertise that can replace all of them.

The first part of the video says AI code doesn't scale....

My brain, "Then I should not show you what my application does because you won't believe it."

My initial reaction says everything. The video's example of "AI code that doesn't scale" was a search box that queries the database on every keystroke. That's a junior oversight on a tutorial project.

What I have built operates at a microscopic level, processes data in real time, runs a full trinary processing pipeline across multiple layers simultaneously, and was designed from day one to operate in government and enterprise environments.

That's not a search box. The person in the video doesn't have a reference point for what I am describing, which is exactly why my instinct is to stay quiet about it.

I am a developer/software engineer's worst nightmare come true.

That said, yes AI will aid  developers making their work faster, but it can also make them obsolete all together at the same time because someone like me exists in the IT Professional world.  TL:DR I understand your domain scope, do you understand mine?

As IT guy with 25+ years of experience - here is my take.
Software Engineering is very - VERY - practical discipline. And when you're spending a day looking how to fix the problem, reading forums, trying something, breaking things down the road, then fixing them, then trying again - it's actually you're learning. AI is definitely is very powerful tool - but it's just a tool. And like with any other tool you need to be qualified to use it. And the only way to get this qualification - you need practice. Practice in hands-on coding, software design, problem solving and so on.

comments.text: I'm doing this for 35 years now, started with Pascal on a 286 with a monochrome-green CRT. I don't really see how juniors will get a foot on the ground nowadays. An example prompt: "Give me an example implementation of rusqlite's ToSql trait for two enums, one with enum values mapping to string fields in database, one mapping to integer fields in database". The problem is: There is no way a junior could write the prompt this way because he does not even know what he actually wants. comments.text: I want to share my journey: I started as a web developer without any real-world project experience. After building two small freelance projects for real customers, I began using AI not just to write code, but as a mentor to learn architecture, design patterns, new languages, libraries, SQL, vector databases, and so much more. So, don’t be lazy and don’t make excuses like 'AI will replace software engineers, so there’s no need to learn to code.' Build your own projects, show them to companies (be aggressive, don't fear rejection), and make your dream job a reality!

comments.author: @tangerinepopgames
comments.text: I started a project as a test back in the summer with no prior knowledge/experience of coding with AI. Lots of amazing realizations, and also some serious challenges.  However, as I became more familiar, in 6 months I was able to bring an app to alpha, in python, typescript and deploy it on a droplet, none of which I have ever used in my professional career.  Because I know and understand system architecture, I was able to get AI to do what I wanted, but that also was a process of creating my commands and guardrails.  I am also paying for a $200 month subscription in order to process all my requests.  The flip side, by AI's estimations, I did in about 1000 hours what would have taken a team of 3 (senior developer and 2 competent coders) appox 2.5 years.  So I would say the acceleration  rate in my experience is somewere between 12:1 andd 18:1 based on the analysis both myself and the AI have done in human hours.   Yes you can get it to do some jobs autonomously, but the less you are engaged with what AI is doing in each process, the more likely you are going to end up with a mess and iterating over the bad code to either remove or fix it.  Also I can confirm that AI is EXTEMELY good with db/backend.  This process went so fast it literally blew my mind.  Where it struggles is with frontend development, and things slow down a bit.  Unit and Mock testing is also very fast and again I was quite impressed.   My takeaway from this video is the overall analysis as to where and how AI fits in is very accurate and I have over 1000 hours in.  As for languages I am familiar with, or projects I have coded myself, it's an invaluable tool for debugging and optimizing.  But again, you have to understand architecture, all the actors involved and where your separations of concerns lie.  AI likes to make assumptions about what you are doing and thats where it gets you in trouble.

comments.text: Btw, one programming language will never prevail because of a number of fundamental features of programming languages: 1) there's no truly general-purpose language, not even machine code since there is no single machine code. There are different CPU architectures for multiple fundamental reasons and just as many machine code languages. And there are many, many more higher level languages, several "general purpose" ones among them none of which is truly general purpose. That is unlikely to ever happen. 2) programming languages need to maintain featureset constraints in order to be practical. A language with too many features becomes unusable and more prone to error. This is especially true while humans are to review code. But even with no humans a language that has thousands of features will have to compromise a lot of efficiency in many areas and you'd end up with multiple issues. I'm not even sure you can have one language encompassing every great feature of every language out there. Human languages can't be like that, nor do I think artificial languages can. comments.author: @UjjwalManandhar
comments.text:
I think of this in the same way we think about compilers. Before compilers existed, people had to write programs directly in assembly language. Even after compilers were introduced, there was a period when developers still needed to understand assembly to debug issues. I remember when I first started with Objective-C for iOS—I often had to dive into assembly to troubleshoot reference counting problems.

Over time, compilers became so powerful and efficient that most developers no longer think about assembly at all. I see LLMs following a similar trajectory. Right now, they don’t always produce production-ready code, and it still makes sense to understand the internals of programming languages. But as these models continue to improve, I believe we’ll reach a point where most developers won’t need deep knowledge of those internals anymore.

Written by me. ( rephrased by LLM)

Right now, the issue isn’t capability, it’s context. Models for example, already know MVVM, SOLID, clean architecture, and how to use specific APIs, but they won’t apply them, unless you explicitly tell them to. If you leave things open, they’ll make decisions for you... Which may not match your intent or business goals. But that’s not a hard limitation, it just means the model needs clearer constraints.
Once you provide that context, AI can already produce systems close to a trained engineer’s level. And as models improve at inferring intent, retaining context, and operating within predefined constraints, that gap disappears. comments.text:
In a bubble, given infinite funding and time and source text, it's almost inevitable for LLMs to improve in how they perform at creating code that builds faster and more efficiently binaries. But there are problems in the premise there. First, nobody is saying that the next level of tools will cost the same. They are in the early times of charging less than what these tools cost or what they are worth, and that is due for a correction. It's early UBER days for LLMs. Second, training data is now scarce, and model collapse may be imminent. We have created 50 years of coding knowledge in the last 50 years, and it'll be another 10 until humans double it, but now much of that will be LLM written. Third, there could be legislative walls on natural/power resource usage and legislative walls on copyrights. Patents exist for human generated work, does an LLM generated codebase meet that standard? And it can reproduce open source licensed code because it was in the training data, but in projects that are the wrong license, and maybe courts will find a lot of projects in breach of GPL. Depends on how much money is on the table for those last three. And it's the entire economy at this point so it's the least worrying, but it exists.

That said, as it exists now, it is disrupting industry. It's not the real reason layoffs were happening, those were mostly economic in nature, things to do with pandemic staffing practices and interest rates. But we do have a talent glut, and people will be competing soon. In the world of tomorrow, everything will have wifi. Someone is building that code, and it will probably be one guy with a herd of LLMs per division for every product and company out there, so that's probably the future to work towards. So we can't just ignore it and wait for the industry to go back. We have to compete against the 100k recently let go developers who are all using this off time to learn LLMs to go faster. That's the reality we need to react to.

It’s funny - as a developer, I’d like to write code and solve problems myself in the future. I’ve tested Codex and other tools quite a few times, and yes, they can deliver excellent results when used by an experienced developer. I’ve also noticed that I get increasingly exhausted when I work a lot with AIs, unlike when I do it myself. Using and monitoring an AI takes up much more energy than when I do it myself. comments.text:
Such engaging content, I feel like a bobblehead dog every time I watch one of your videos :D
It literally gave me the shivers, you know the feeling when somebody manages to explain so clearly what you had in your head for a long time.

I've been thinking about this phenomenon myself as well. For some time, I felt that systems change faster than teams can agree on what must remain true.
One way I'm trying to frame this problem is through the lens of divergence and convergence: exploration followed by consolidation. Healthy systems need both forces. When they fall out of balance, entropy creeps in. I find it fascinating that - kinda following the law of physics - code also has a tendency towards disorder over time.
When divergence becomes so cheap, one needs an equal counterweight to balance the scales, and a CI/CD system you described, or a well-crafted agentic harness with a fast feedback loop is exactly that force! 

I hope you don't mind, but when something resonates so well with my own thoughts, I feel like I must share. I wrote a blog post about this exact feeling, and your video gives such a neat, practical framing of it, like the other half of the same coin:  https://www.abelenekes.com/p/when-change-becomes-cheaper-than-commitment

I'm so glad there's a community like the MSE team, who have a practical, measured stance on AI and actively investigates how well proven SWE best practices can assist us in this age! 

Thank you for all your work and teaching!

Well, the problem is there is a marked distinction between software engineering as a disciplinary science, and what we call software developers (and I think you're calling software engineers like what those what stoked coal into steam engines).  The likely fact is software engineering (like a lot of good ideas) does not survive contact with industrial practices, because of the WISCY principle.  That and people to often lean into what is happening with software coding under duress and call it software engineering.  You'll find the problem is the rush to generate code, in the industry, is way more reactionary and disruptive and so is it really engineering, since you can't build a sky scraper that way. 

The closest analogy is actually to give 1000 brick layers a pile of bricks each, say "ready steady GO!" and accept the emergent properties of the system as a building - essentially the way Agile really works.

So, don't get me wrong, I wrote code that worked but does that make me an engineer or an artesan? 

So, be real, AI is built on a corpus of median quality heuristic code from github with personnel taste applied with tuning for training.

Vibe coding is analoguous to the coding of early nasa endeavours, before Margaret Hamilton sorted NASA out.

We are really resetting back to the necessities of software engineering, especially requirements engineering, by which I don't mean user stories (analogous to vibe coding prompts for AI and why SDD is now the best new thing on the block though it reaks of the insidious "Water Fall" right, since we didn't like that idea).

So, my take, since AI is trained on a corpus of code often generated, in the first place, without explict user requirements, and nor refined to specifications (that would make sense for getting anything useful out of TDD), it is still likely  an embodiment of thost accidental concepts to be recovered with super stimulas in the prompting (something SSD is not, given SSD is the best evidence we still don't have an applied engineering science behind requirements engineering) - but only for the slop that went into the training.

The point being, context is king and if the corpus has it you can recover it, abliet as a stochastic and non-determinstic set of tokens, a mear shadow of the original, but any software lead will recount the same experience with those minions they have managed over the years.

Now, that idea, that we could recover software engineered code, would be way more plausible if the software AI was trained upon was software that was software engineered.

So if the complaint is AI is regurgitating the hueristic slop we created for the sake of the mantra of free software, sans the engineering science, sucked in, suck it up, and do the software engineering. comments.text:
I think “AI won’t replace software engineering” is true, but maybe not because AI is only a coding tool.

The deeper issue is that software engineering is not just code production. It is context, judgment, tradeoffs, history, responsibility, and knowing which “correct” fix is dangerous in the real system.

When AI fails at coding, people often focus on the bad output.

But the more interesting question is:

“What was missing from the situation that made this bad output possible?”

A human engineer does not work from code alone. They carry architecture, production experience, team conventions, past failures, and invisible constraints. Much of engineering skill is not in typing the code, but in knowing what the code means inside a living system.

So maybe the future question is not whether AI can write code.

It is whether our systems are understandable enough for any intelligence, human or artificial, to safely act on them.

That is where I think the debate gets interesting.

comments.text: I have done quite a lot of AI-augmented software engineering recently. Every couple of months, the level at which I need to manage it jumps up a level. It went from being good for smart autocomplete to being good at generating boilerplate, to knowing weird computer science tricks for bit twiddling that could be used deep down in a data structure, to being able to propose and carry out complex refactorings, and onwards and upwards. It will still, if not given oversight, generate a ball of repetitive mud. but that's reducing each generation of AI. We can tell ourselves that our skills will always be needed, but if this carries on in the trajectory that it has been, I don't actually think that will be a safe bet. My AI workflows use continuously tested small steps, always-running systems, testing from unit to integration to full app, all automated, and the agents write nearly as much scaffolding documentation as code. And unlike that documentation if it was written and maintained by humans, the agents will keep the text and code in sync. Increasingly, the AI understands the domain space well, particularly after discussions and feed back on small feature-specific wireframes or prototypes. No different, really, than what you'd do with other members of your development team. Increasingly, I spend the majority of my time thinking about hard problems and then talking them through with the agent until that is rigorously described. But from then on, the agents can do a better job of getting that up and running than I could achieve with a small, relatively good developer team.

​Pattern Analysis
​Redundancy: The "will AI replace programmers" narrative is a saturated pattern. It lacks the raw mechanics of the how; it focuses on the "why" and the "when" of social impact, which violates the Truth Over Comfort directive by leaning into emotional speculation (anxiety over money/jobs).

comments.author: @Oldrich333
comments.text:
This is an absolutely misleading example regarding radiology and a textbook lie. Jensen ignores hard data about the global workforce: roughly 60% of employees bring no added value, and another 15% actively act against the company, creating losses. These 75% are essentially redundant. AI will not merely 'change their tools'; AI will simply filter them out and replace them.

Furthermore, regarding radiologists, he is comparing apples to oranges. The AI he mentions in relation to 2020 was narrowly specialized computer vision. It could find a tumor, but it couldn't establish a complex diagnosis or write a medical report. Human intervention was necessary both factually and legally.

However, with today's LLM assistants, even that factual necessity has fallen away. AI can now handle data synthesis, context, and report writing. The only thing genuinely left for the human is legal liability. A radiologist today essentially functions like a COO—formally adding a signature to a decision and bearing responsibility for it, but almost all the actual work has already been done by something else. Comparing this narrow, legally protected top-tier group to the general workforce, where no such safeguard exists, is a total illusion. The vast majority will be replaced, and very quickly.

References:

Gallup - State of the Global Workplace Reports: Consistent data on 15% of employees being "actively disengaged" (working against the firm) and ~60% "not engaged" (adding no special value).

The Vitality Curve (Jack Welch/GE): The established "20-70-10" rule identifying the bottom 10% as underperformers causing net losses.

Price’s Law: A common statistical model in organizations showing that 50% of work is produced by the square root of the total number of employees (meaning the vast majority contribute minimal value).

comments.author: @UponGiantsShoulders
comments.text:
I am a systems engineer with 25 years of experience. I’ve always resented the need to learn code to be effective in my role. I do have a good knowledge of PowerShell and SQL and have a solid understanding of object-oriented programming, but it still feels like pulling teeth to sit down and work line by line to create, update, or fix code.

I spent eight years as an application support engineer, working in SQL every day. Even then, anything beyond updating a report or comparing a few tables felt onerous—because writing code and doing support are fundamentally different kinds of work. My focus was always on the next ticket or making tools to help resolve the next ticket, not on deepening my familiarity with a new library or refining my coding skills.

Since the rise of AI, I’ve started shifting into a more design-centered approach to get the most out of it, and that’s been essential. More than anything else, that shift has pulled me back into learning code—but from a different angle. By asking critical questions about why something works the way it does, AI helps surface the missing pieces that connect the dots.

Design is engaging. It provides context and intent. Coding, on its own, still isn’t something I naturally gravitate toward—but when it’s driven by design, it finally feels purposeful.

It is reasonable to approach some of the public messaging around artificial intelligence with caution. In certain cases, executive statements about AI appear to be driven more by the expectations of investors and financial markets than by the practical realities faced by software developers and the broader engineering community. While AI technologies are advancing rapidly and offer meaningful opportunities, overstated claims can create unrealistic expectations about timelines, capabilities, and impact.

Sustainable progress in AI depends not only on market enthusiasm but also on the contributions of researchers, engineers, and developers who build, test, and maintain these systems. A balanced perspective one that recognizes both the potential and the limitations of AI is essential for responsible innovation and long-term value creation.

comments.author: @PeterOeC
comments.text:
There has to be a skilled developer in the loop when working with agents, otherwise you won't catch the moment where the AI goes slightly off the path you intend, and you end up with a solution that is hard to maintain, or contains bugs or vulnerabilities, it is not appropriate for the problem at hand.

Sure agents can be a productivity booster if done correctly, but it doesn't totally replace software engineers all together, and you still have to be good at managing context, tell it the right intentions, and catch it if it's doing a bad job.
Also if you start using AI to your advantage in your company, you might have a slight advantage over other companies who's not currently using AI. But when the other companies start using AI as well your company doesn't have an advantage any longer, and then you need more software engineers to keep up, cause the "software engineers with AI" is the new normal.
There's been countless of tools introduced throughout time. Computers, internet, Microsoft Teams, Excel, Word, Outlook. They all change how we work. And people work more efficient, but all these things is the new normal now, and every worker is using them. I think the same thing will happen with AI.
People were also afraid that computers would replace them back when they were introduced, but you still need the person operating the computer.

My advice as a mid-to-high level software engineer, is to try to not be stressed about AI. It's a relatively new technology. Tools are evolving crazy fast, it's hard to keep up with the newest developments. But EVERYONE feels the same way: "Oh sh*t, is everyone besides me doing AI right now!? Am I going extinct?! What about all my skills and education?!" 

Don't worry. Keep an eye on AI. Try it out, see if it can do just one repetitive task you used to do, or help you in some way. Then you learn how to use it, you see more ways to use it gradually. And tools will only become better and easy to work with as time passes.

AI is not perfect. It's like a wild horse that you need to steer and keep on the path of intentions. If you let it run free, you'll end up in the forrest, and you'll have to spend a lot of time getting back to the path. But if you can steer it left or right and keep it on the path, you might be slightly faster than the seasoned runner, who does things efficiently and manually himself.
We're used to running, and doing things efficiently by ourselves, but now we need to learn to ride horses, and we don't learn that in 1 day. But eventually everyone's gonna ride horses, and it'll be easy, and the new normal. But don't stress about not knowing how to ride horses yet - don't stress about not knowing how to use agents efficiently yet. But try tinker with it, and keep an eye on it. And learn from your coworkers.

Good insight - learn the key all-rounder pillars and find a way to show you know them :) The key skillsets aka "the practice" of an Architect Mindset are:

1. dev and computer science and patterns and math
2. infra - cloud and real
3. Business Analysis
4. Data Science, data design
5. Specialist tech areas of depth, aka domains - AI, but also finance, media, networking, cyber etc
and then the overlap with the people managers
6. Network of peers and stakeholders
7. deeper business skills - quals that stakeholders also have
8. project/team management - even agents need team structure and governance
9. last and not least, document engineering and 
10. live presentation skills

You need to ladder up your skills in many areas and show you have

You can now see the ring fence in the AI era - not one human skill, but lots

If devs want to follow the Individual Contributor path, the career is more all round skills, unlike people managers who can focus more on those number 6-10 GM skills
